sujet:
Practice paper – Essay writing

In many neighbourhoods of our towns, young people complain about unemployment, while law enforcement officers note a rise in petty crime.

What links can be established between youth unemployment and insecurity in our towns? As a future police inspector, what solutions would you propose to reduce this problem?

Illustrate your answer with precise examples from Cameroonian society.
corrige:
Cameroon has a very young population: more than half of its inhabitants are under twenty-five. This youth should be the strength of the nation, yet many young people leave school or university and find no stable job. At the same time, in cities such as Douala and Yaoundé, residents complain about bag snatching, night-time attacks, burglaries and drug dealing. Is there, then, a link between youth unemployment and the insecurity observed in our towns, and what can a police inspector do to reduce this problem? We shall first analyse the links between unemployment and insecurity, showing that unemployment encourages crime without being its only cause, and then propose solutions involving the police, the public authorities and society as a whole.

There is a real link between youth unemployment and insecurity in our towns, although unemployment alone cannot explain the rise in petty crime.

Firstly, unemployment creates idleness and poverty, which make some young people vulnerable to crime. A young person without income or occupation spends the whole day in the street, while the pressure of daily needs remains: food, rent, school fees for younger brothers and sisters. Some then look for easy money through theft, receiving stolen goods or online scams, the well-known "feymania". For instance, mobile phones snatched in the street are often resold cheaply in informal markets by young people who have no other source of income.

Moreover, long-term unemployment destroys self-esteem and pushes some young people towards gangs. A young graduate who has sent dozens of applications without success may feel useless and rejected by society. In a gang, he finds the recognition, the protection and the sense of belonging that society does not give him. This explains why, in some popular neighbourhoods of Douala and Yaoundé, groups of idle young people armed with knives attack passers-by at night and defend "their" territory.

However, unemployment does not explain everything. The great majority of unemployed young people remain honest: they work as bike riders, hawkers, apprentices or call-box operators to earn a living with dignity. Other factors therefore play a decisive role, such as drug abuse, especially tramadol and cannabis, which makes young people aggressive and fearless; weak parental supervision; the rural exodus, which leaves young people without family ties in the city; and impunity, when offenders are released without punishment and return to the neighbourhood as models.

In short, unemployment is fertile ground for insecurity, but it combines with drugs, family breakdown and impunity. Since the causes are multiple, the solutions must also be multiple, and this is what we shall now consider.

The response to insecurity linked to youth unemployment must combine firmness and prevention, and it must involve the police, the State, the councils and the community.

Firstly, the police inspector has a central role to play on the ground. He must ensure a visible presence through regular patrols in sensitive areas, especially at night, and report dark spots to the councils so that street lights can be installed. He must also develop community policing by working with quarter heads, vigilance committees, youth associations and religious leaders, in order to gather information and prevent crime rather than only repress it. Furthermore, he must firmly dismantle the drug and fencing networks that exploit young people, while treating every young person with respect, because a humiliated young man rarely becomes a cooperative citizen.

Moreover, the State and the councils must offer young people real alternatives to crime. Existing programmes such as the National Employment Fund and PIAASI, which supports actors of the informal sector, should be better known in the neighbourhoods. Vocational training centres can teach practical trades such as welding, sewing, mechanics or computer maintenance. In addition, councils can create labour-intensive public works, for example cleaning gutters, maintaining roads or collecting rubbish, which give young people both an income and a feeling of usefulness.

Finally, families and civil society must take part in the effort. Parents must guide and supervise their children, while schools and churches promote civic and moral values. Sports and cultural activities, such as neighbourhood football tournaments or the activities organised around the National Youth Day on 11 February, keep young people usefully busy and help them discover their talents. Thus, prevention becomes the business of the whole community.

In conclusion, youth unemployment is clearly a breeding ground for insecurity in our towns, because it creates idleness, poverty and frustration; nevertheless, it is not the only cause, since drugs, weak family supervision and impunity also play a part. The answer must therefore combine firm police action and long-term prevention through employment, training and education. As a future police inspector, I am convinced that security cannot be achieved by repression alone, but by working hand in hand with the population. Is it not true that tomorrow's security will be built as much through jobs as through law enforcement?

———
How this answer is built:
– Lead-in: “Cameroon has a very young population: more than half of its inhabitants are under twenty-five.”
– Problem: “Is there, then, a link between youth unemployment and the insecurity observed in our towns…”
– Plan outline: “We shall first analyse the links between unemployment and insecurity…”
– Part one (main idea): “There is a real link between youth unemployment and insecurity in our towns…”
– Transition: “Since the causes are multiple, the solutions must also be multiple…”
– Part two (main idea): “The response to insecurity linked to youth unemployment must combine firmness and prevention…”
– Summary: “In conclusion, youth unemployment is clearly a breeding ground for insecurity in our towns…”
– Answer to the problem: “As a future police inspector, I am convinced that security cannot be achieved by repression alone…”
– Opening: “Is it not true that tomorrow's security will be built as much through jobs…”

sujet:
Practice paper – General knowledge

PART A – Questions (10 marks)
1. What is the political capital of Cameroon and what is its economic capital? (1 mark)
2. How many regions does Cameroon have? Name five. (2 marks)
3. What are the two official languages of Cameroon? (1 mark)
4. In which year did British Southern Cameroons vote in the plebiscite, and what was the result? (2 marks)
5. What does DGSN stand for? (1 mark)
6. Define police custody (garde à vue). (3 marks)

PART B – Essay (10 marks)
"A police officer is first and foremost at the service of the citizen." Discuss.
corrige:
PART A – QUESTIONS

Question 1 (1 mark): What is the political capital of Cameroon and what is its economic capital?
Answer: The political capital of Cameroon is Yaoundé, where the main State institutions (the Presidency, the National Assembly and the ministries) are located, and its economic capital is Douala, the country's main port and industrial city.
Marks: 0.5 mark for Yaoundé, 0.5 mark for Douala.

Question 2 (2 marks): How many regions does Cameroon have? Name five.
Answer: Cameroon has ten regions, namely Adamawa, Centre, East, Far North, Littoral, North, North West, West, South and South West; these former provinces were renamed regions by a decree in 2008.
Marks: 1 mark for the correct number (ten), 0.2 mark per correct region up to five (1 mark).

Question 3 (1 mark): What are the two official languages of Cameroon?
Answer: The two official languages of Cameroon are English and French, which the Constitution recognises as having equal status; this bilingualism reflects the country's history, as parts of it were administered by Britain and France.
Marks: 0.5 mark per correct language.

Question 4 (2 marks): In which year did British Southern Cameroons vote in the plebiscite, and what was the result?
Answer: British Southern Cameroons voted in the plebiscite in 1961, on 11 February 1961, and the result was a clear majority (about 70 per cent) in favour of joining the Republic of Cameroun, which led to reunification on 1 October 1961; in the separate vote, Northern Cameroons chose to join Nigeria.
Marks: 1 mark for 1961, 1 mark for the result (joining the Republic of Cameroun); mentioning reunification on 1 October 1961 is appreciated but not required.

Question 5 (1 mark): What does DGSN stand for?
Answer: DGSN stands for Délégation Générale à la Sûreté Nationale (General Delegation for National Security), the administration that heads the Cameroon national police under the authority of a Delegate General.
Marks: 1 mark for the exact French expansion (the English translation alone earns 0.5 mark).

Question 6 (3 marks): Define police custody (garde à vue).
Answer: Police custody (garde à vue) is a police measure by which a judicial police officer holds a person suspected of having committed an offence at a police or gendarmerie station for the needs of the investigation; under the 2005 Cameroon Criminal Procedure Code (sections 119 and following), it lasts 48 hours, renewable once with the authorisation of the State Counsel (procureur de la République), and the person in custody keeps certain rights, in particular to be informed of the facts alleged, to inform his family, to be visited by his lawyer and to be examined by a doctor.
Marks: 1 mark for the definition (ordered by a judicial police officer, suspect held, needs of the investigation), 1 mark for the duration and supervision by the State Counsel, 1 mark for at least two rights of the person in custody.

PART B – ESSAY

Topic: "A police officer is first and foremost at the service of the citizen." Discuss.

For many Cameroonians, the police officer is first of all the man at the checkpoint, the one who stops vehicles, asks for papers and sometimes makes arrests, in other words a figure of authority rather than of help. Yet the statement that "a police officer is first and foremost at the service of the citizen" reminds us that the public force exists only to protect the population. Is the police officer really a servant of the citizen, or does his role of authority sometimes set him apart from the people he is meant to serve? We shall first show that serving the citizen is the very purpose of the police, before examining the limits that weaken this mission and the ways to overcome them.

Serving the citizen is indeed the very purpose of the police. First, the police officer protects people's lives and property: through day and night patrols he deters criminals, and he intervenes quickly when a call to 117 reports a theft or an assault. Secondly, he guarantees public freedoms, because it is thanks to his presence that citizens can move about, trade and vote safely, as the security arrangements set up at every election show. Finally, he is the first link in the justice chain: he receives complaints, records offences and conducts investigations that allow victims to obtain redress. Thus, through protection, the guarantee of freedoms and investigation, the police officer works first for the good of the citizen. However, a principle is only as good as its application.

On the ground, this mission of service is not always perceived, nor always fulfilled. In the first place, the misconduct of some officers, such as corruption during road checks or excessive use of force, damages public trust and gives the image of a police force that serves itself instead of serving others. In the second place, the shortage of staff and equipment limits police presence in some outlying neighbourhoods and rural areas, where residents feel abandoned. Moreover, the officer must sometimes restrain the citizen, for example by fining him or placing him in custody; yet this restraint, framed by law, is itself a service to the community. This is why the authorities respond with ethics and human-rights training, sanctions against misbehaving officers and the development of community policing with a better welcome in police stations.

In short, the police officer is indeed first and foremost at the service of the citizen, since all his missions aim at protecting people, property and freedoms. Nevertheless, this vocation is fully achieved only when the officer acts with integrity and has the means to do his job. The force entrusted to him by law is therefore not a privilege but a responsibility. It remains to be seen whether citizens, for their part, are ready to cooperate with the police, since security can never be built without them.

———
How this answer is built:
Lead-in: "For many Cameroonians, the police officer is first of all the man at the checkpoint…"
Problem: "Is the police officer really a servant of the citizen, or does his role of authority…"
Plan outline: "We shall first show that serving the citizen is the very purpose of the police, before…"
Part one: "Serving the citizen is indeed the very purpose of the police."
Transition: "Thus, through protection, the guarantee of freedoms and investigation… However, a principle is only as good as its application."
Part two: "On the ground, this mission of service is not always perceived, nor always fulfilled."
Summary: "In short, the police officer is indeed first and foremost at the service of the citizen…"
Answer to the problem: "Nevertheless, this vocation is fully achieved only when the officer acts with integrity…"
Opening: "It remains to be seen whether citizens, for their part, are ready to cooperate with the police…"

sujet:
Practice paper – Essay writing

Social media play a growing role in the lives of young Cameroonians. They inform, but they also spread fake news and hate speech.

Discuss the advantages and dangers of social media, then explain how they can be used responsibly.
corrige:
In only a few years, WhatsApp, Facebook and TikTok have become, for many young Cameroonians, the main source of news, entertainment and even income. A smartphone and a few hundred francs of internet data are now enough to speak to the whole country. Yet the same platforms that inform and connect people also carry rumours, insults and hatred at great speed. What, then, are the advantages and dangers of social media for young Cameroonians, and how can these tools be used responsibly? We shall first weigh the advantages of social media against their dangers, and then show how responsible use can be achieved by individuals, families, schools and the authorities.

Social media offer young Cameroonians real advantages, but they also carry serious dangers for individuals and for society.

Firstly, social media bring people together and give access to information. They connect families scattered between towns, villages and the diaspora: a student in Buea can talk every day with his parents in Garoua or with a brother in Europe. Moreover, they are a powerful source of knowledge and opportunities. Young people follow online courses, discover job offers and learn about competitive entrance examinations, while young entrepreneurs sell clothes, food or cosmetics through WhatsApp statuses and Facebook pages. For many unemployed young people, social media have thus become a shop window and a source of income.

However, social media are also a channel for fake news and hate speech. A false death announcement, an invented decree or a doctored photo can be shared thousands of times within hours, causing panic and sometimes disturbing public order. Even more serious, tribal and political hate speech threatens peaceful coexistence in a country of great ethnic diversity. This is why Law No. 2019/020 of 24 December 2019, amending the Penal Code, punishes contempt of tribes or ethnic groups, and why the spreading of false news is also an offence under Cameroonian law.

Furthermore, social media expose young people to cybercrime and addiction. Scams, hacked accounts, identity theft and blackmail with intimate photos make many victims, often naive teenagers. In addition, many students spend a large part of the night scrolling on TikTok or chatting on WhatsApp, and they arrive in class tired and unable to concentrate. Thus, a tool meant to open the mind can end up imprisoning it.

In short, social media are a precious tool for communication, learning and business, but they can also spread lies, hatred and crime. Since the problem lies less in the tool itself than in the way it is used, we must now examine how young Cameroonians can use social media responsibly.

Responsible use of social media depends first on each user, but also on families, schools and the public authorities.

Firstly, every user must adopt simple digital reflexes. Before sharing a piece of information, he must check its source and compare it with official channels, for example consulting the official website of a ministry for examination results instead of trusting a screenshot. He must refuse to forward hateful or insulting messages, protect his personal data and passwords, and never send intimate images. Moreover, he should limit his screen time so that social media remain a tool and not a master.

Moreover, families and schools have an educational role to play. Parents must take an interest in what their children do online and set rules for the use of phones. Schools can teach digital citizenship, showing students how to recognise fake news and how to behave respectfully online. In this respect, the awareness campaigns of the National Agency for Information and Communication Technologies (ANTIC) on cybersecurity deserve to be extended to all secondary schools.

Finally, the authorities and the police must prevent and punish abuses, while respecting freedom of expression. Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on cybersecurity and cybercriminality provides a legal framework against online offences, and specialised units can investigate scams and blackmail. Citizens, for their part, should report hateful content to the platforms and serious offences to the police. As for the future police officer, he must set the example by never using social media to insult, to spread rumours or to publish confidential information about his service.

In conclusion, social media bring real benefits to young Cameroonians in terms of communication, education and business, but they also spread fake news, hate speech and cybercrime and can lead to addiction. Their responsible use relies on the vigilance of each user, on education by families and schools, and on the firm but fair action of the authorities. In my opinion, social media are neither good nor bad in themselves: everything depends on the person who uses them. The real question is therefore whether our society will train digital citizens as quickly as technology creates new platforms.

———
How this answer is built:
– Lead-in: “In only a few years, WhatsApp, Facebook and TikTok have become…”
– Problem: “What, then, are the advantages and dangers of social media for young Cameroonians…”
– Plan outline: “We shall first weigh the advantages of social media against their dangers…”
– Part one (main idea): “Social media offer young Cameroonians real advantages, but they also carry serious dangers…”
– Transition: “Since the problem lies less in the tool itself than in the way it is used…”
– Part two (main idea): “Responsible use of social media depends first on each user…”
– Summary: “In conclusion, social media bring real benefits to young Cameroonians…”
– Answer to the problem: “In my opinion, social media are neither good nor bad in themselves…”
– Opening: “The real question is therefore whether our society will train digital citizens…”

sujet:
Practice paper – Essay writing

Road accidents claim many victims on Cameroon's roads every year.

What are their main causes? As a future police constable, what would you propose to reduce these accidents?
corrige:
Every week, newspapers, radio stations and social media report serious accidents on Cameroon's roads, especially on the Douala–Yaoundé road and in our big towns, where commercial motorbikes are often involved. These accidents kill and injure many people, leave families in mourning and cost the country a lot of money. Why are there so many accidents on our roads, and what can a police constable do to reduce them? In this essay, we shall first examine the main causes of road accidents, and then propose solutions that a future police constable and other actors can put into practice.

Road accidents in Cameroon have several causes, which come from road users, from vehicles and from the state of the roads.

Firstly, the behaviour of drivers is the leading cause of accidents. Many drivers drive too fast, overtake on bends or on hills, and do not respect the highway code. Some drink alcohol before driving or use their phones at the wheel. Long-distance bus drivers are often tired because they drive at night without rest. For example, on the Douala–Yaoundé road, many head-on collisions happen when a driver overtakes a truck without seeing the vehicle coming in front.

Moreover, many vehicles are in poor condition. They run on worn tyres or with faulty brakes and lights, and some have no valid roadworthiness test. In addition, buses and trucks are often overloaded with passengers and goods, which makes them difficult to control. In some motor parks, for instance, small cars carry more passengers than the law allows, and luggage is piled high on the roof.

Furthermore, the state of the roads and the disregard for rules make the situation worse. Potholes, poor lighting and missing road signs surprise drivers, especially at night and in the rainy season. In our towns, many bike riders have no driving licence, wear no helmet and carry two or three passengers at the same time. Thus, the smallest mistake can become a tragedy.

In short, road accidents are caused by human behaviour, by vehicles in poor condition and by bad roads. Now that we know these causes, we can look at the solutions that can reduce the number of accidents.

To reduce road accidents, the police constable must play his part with firmness and honesty, but he also needs the help of other actors.

Firstly, the police constable must carry out regular and serious checks. He can check speed and the alcohol level of drivers, and he must verify vehicle documents such as the driving licence, the insurance certificate and the roadworthiness certificate. He must also sanction overloading and bike riders without helmets. Above all, he must be honest: a check that can be bought with a small bribe lets a dangerous vehicle go back on the road and puts lives in danger.

Moreover, prevention is as important as punishment. The police constable can take part in awareness campaigns in motor parks, in schools and with bike riders' unions. He can explain the dangers of speeding, drink-driving and phones at the wheel. These campaigns are particularly useful before the end-of-year holidays, when traffic increases and many people travel to their villages.

Finally, other actors must also play their part. The State and the councils must repair roads, put up road signs and install street lights. Driving schools must train their students seriously instead of selling licences. Vehicle owners must maintain their cars, and passengers must refuse to travel in an overloaded vehicle or with a drunk driver.

In conclusion, road accidents in Cameroon are caused by the bad behaviour of road users, by vehicles in poor condition and by bad roads. To reduce them, strict and honest checks and good awareness campaigns are necessary, together with the efforts of the State, driving schools and all road users. As a future police constable, I believe that a disciplined and honest officer can save many lives. However, will our roads become safe if every road user does not decide to respect the highway code?

sujet:
Practice paper – General knowledge (questions)

1. What is the motto of Cameroon? (2 marks)
2. What are the colours of the Cameroon flag and what is on the central stripe? (2 marks)
3. Which number do you dial to reach the police in Cameroon? (1 mark)
4. Name four countries that share a border with Cameroon. (2 marks)
5. On what date is National Day celebrated? (1 mark)
6. What is an identity document? Give two examples. (2 marks)
7. What is the role of a police constable? (4 marks)
8. Give three rights and three duties of a citizen. (6 marks)
corrige:
Question 1 (2 marks): What is the motto of Cameroon?
Answer: The motto of Cameroon is "Peace – Work – Fatherland" (in French, "Paix – Travail – Patrie"); written into the Constitution, it expresses the values on which the nation intends to build itself.
Marks: 2 marks for the complete motto in the correct order, 1 mark if the order is wrong, 0 if a word is missing or incorrect.

Question 2 (2 marks): What are the colours of the Cameroon flag and what is on the central stripe?
Answer: The colours of the Cameroon flag are green, red and yellow, arranged in three equal vertical stripes, and the red central stripe bears a gold (yellow) five-pointed star in its centre, a symbol of national unity.
Marks: 0.5 mark per correct colour (1.5 marks), 0.5 mark for the yellow five-pointed star on the red stripe.

Question 3 (1 mark): Which number do you dial to reach the police in Cameroon?
Answer: To reach the police in Cameroon, you dial 117; this emergency number is free of charge, while the gendarmerie can be reached on 113 and the fire brigade on 118.
Marks: 1 mark for 117.

Question 4 (2 marks): Name four countries that share a border with Cameroon.
Answer: Cameroon shares its borders with six countries, namely Nigeria to the west, Chad to the north, the Central African Republic to the east, and Congo, Gabon and Equatorial Guinea to the south; to the south-west it opens onto the Atlantic Ocean (Gulf of Guinea).
Marks: 0.5 mark per correct country, up to four.

Question 5 (1 mark): On what date is National Day celebrated?
Answer: Cameroon's National Day is celebrated on 20 May; it commemorates the referendum of 20 May 1972, which created the unitary State (the United Republic of Cameroon), hence its name of National Unity Day.
Marks: 1 mark for 20 May.

Question 6 (2 marks): What is an identity document? Give two examples.
Answer: An identity document is an official document issued by a public authority that proves a person's identity (surname, first names, date and place of birth, photograph); in Cameroon the main examples are the national identity card, issued by the DGSN, and the passport, while the residence permit plays this role for foreign residents.
Marks: 1 mark for the definition (official document proving identity), 0.5 mark per correct example, up to two.

Question 7 (4 marks): What is the role of a police constable?
Answer: The role of a police constable is to ensure, on the ground, the safety of people and property and the maintenance of public order; in practice, he patrols, controls road traffic, records offences and arrests offenders, assists people in danger, guards public buildings and takes part in public-order operations, while staying in direct contact with the population under the authority of his superiors.
Marks: 1 mark for the general mission (safety of people and property, public order), 0.5 mark per correct concrete task, up to six (3 marks).

Question 8 (6 marks): Give three rights and three duties of a citizen.
Answer: A Cameroonian citizen's rights include the right to life and security, the right to education and the right to vote (as well as freedom of expression or the right to health), and his duties include obeying the law and respecting institutions, paying taxes and defending the nation (as well as respecting public property and other people); rights and duties go together, because enjoying one's rights means respecting those of others.
Marks: 1 mark per correct right (3 marks) and 1 mark per correct duty (3 marks).

sujet:
Practice paper – General knowledge (essay)

"A leader is someone who needs others." (Paul Valéry)

Discuss this statement using examples from history, military life and Cameroonian society.
corrige:
The traditional image of the leader is that of a solitary figure: the general on horseback overlooking the battlefield, the statesman deciding alone in his office. Charles de Gaulle himself wrote in The Edge of the Sword (1932) that there is no authority without prestige, and no prestige without distance. Paul Valéry, however, reverses this image when he states that "a leader is someone who needs others". In his view, what defines the leader is not his independence but his dependence on those he leads. Is command, then, essentially a relationship of dependence on others, or does the leader remain the one who, in the end, decides and answers alone? We shall first show that the leader truly needs others, for his strength, his information and his legitimacy; we shall then see that this dependence does not dissolve his responsibility, since others need him just as much, which turns command into a form of service.

Valéry's statement first expresses a profound truth: a leader exists only through others and with others.

Firstly, there is no leader without followers, and no victory without the cohesion of a group. A commander's plans are worth nothing if no one carries them out. Napoleon's victories would have been impossible without the Grande Armée and the talent of his marshals, and he himself insisted that in war the moral factor counts far more than the material one. In military life, an officer is only worth the cohesion of his section or his company; this is why the training of young officers insists so much on team spirit. Cameroonian society offers a similar lesson outside the barracks: the Indomitable Lions reached the quarter-finals of the 1990 World Cup not through one individual alone, but because the experience of Roger Milla was supported by a united collective.

Moreover, the leader needs the knowledge and skills of others in order to decide well. Modern warfare is so complex that no single mind can master intelligence, logistics, communications and fire support at the same time. During the Normandy landings of June 1944, Dwight Eisenhower depended on a coalition of allied armies, on his staff and even on his meteorologists, whose forecast of a short break in the weather led him to choose 6 June. In the same way, in the fight against Boko Haram in the Far North region, Cameroonian defence forces have relied heavily on vigilance committees and on local populations, who provide information that no satellite can give.

Furthermore, the leader needs the trust and consent of those he commands. Authority is not simply imposed by rank or decree; it must be recognised. A leader who is merely feared is obeyed as long as he is watching, and his authority collapses under the stress of combat. Traditional societies in Cameroon understood this well: in many chiefdoms of the Grassfields, the Fon does not rule alone but with councils of notables and regulatory societies such as the Kwifon, which advise him and can even restrain him. Legitimacy, in other words, is given by others.

Thus, the leader is indeed someone who needs others: he draws his strength from the group, his lucidity from his advisers and his legitimacy from the trust of those he leads. Yet reducing the leader to a dependent man would ignore an essential aspect of command, namely that others also need him.

However, if the leader needs others, others need him even more: his dependence does not cancel his responsibility, and it gives command its true meaning as a service.

Firstly, the leader is the one who decides and who bears the weight of the decision alone. Advice can be collected, but at the decisive moment someone must choose, often in urgency and uncertainty. On the eve of the Normandy landings, Eisenhower prepared a short note in which he took full personal responsibility in case of failure. Likewise, when de Gaulle launched his appeal of 18 June 1940, he was almost alone; it was his decision that created the Free French movement, and not the other way round. Cameroon was associated with this history, since it was in Douala that Leclerc rallied the territory to Free France in August 1940, before leading from Chad the campaign that ended in the oath of Kufra.

Moreover, the group needs the leader as an example and as a point of reference. In difficult moments, soldiers look at their officer: his calm, his courage and his willingness to share their hardships give them the strength to continue. Nelson Mandela, after twenty-seven years in prison, depended on the support of his comrades and of the international community, but it was his personal example of forgiveness that made national reconciliation possible in South Africa. Without such a figure, a group can easily fall into division or panic.

Finally, going beyond the opposition between dependence and authority, true command appears as a relationship of mutual service. The leader who knows that he needs others listens to them, delegates, trusts the initiative of his subordinates and helps them grow; this is the spirit of mission command in modern armies, where the leader explains his intent and leaves his subordinates free to choose the means. This is also the ideal pursued at EMIA, which trains officers to command by example and to serve the Nation rather than to serve themselves. In many Cameroonian traditions, the chief is likewise seen as the servant of his community, whose prosperity is the measure of his success.

In conclusion, Valéry's statement is profoundly true: a leader depends on others for his strength, his information and the legitimacy of his authority. Nevertheless, this dependence does not reduce him to a simple instrument of the group, because he remains the one who decides, who sets the example and who answers for the outcome. My position is therefore that needing others is not a weakness of the leader but the very condition of his authority, provided he accepts in return to serve those he leads and to bear the responsibility of decision. In an age of digital networks and collective intelligence, where information circulates everywhere, will the leader of tomorrow still be the one who decides, or above all the one who knows how to unite?

sujet:
Practice paper – General culture

Should Cameroonian schools first pass on knowledge or prepare students for a job?

Answer in a well-argued essay.
corrige:
In many Cameroonian towns, it is no longer surprising to meet holders of a bachelor's or even a master's degree working as bike riders, call-box operators or street hawkers. This painful reality of graduate unemployment has revived an old debate about the purpose of education. Montaigne already preferred "a well-made head rather than a well-filled one", while today parents and employers ask schools to produce young people who are immediately employable. Should Cameroonian schools, then, give priority to the transmission of knowledge, or should they first prepare students for a job? We shall first show that the transmission of knowledge remains the fundamental and irreplaceable mission of school; we shall then see that, in the present economic context, school must also prepare for employment, and that the two missions can and must be reconciled.

The transmission of knowledge is the first mission of school, because it lays the foundations of every individual and of the Nation.

Firstly, knowledge provides the basic skills without which no trade can be learnt. Reading, writing, counting, reasoning and understanding the basic laws of the sciences are the foundation of every profession, from the mechanic who reads a technical manual to the farmer who calculates doses of fertiliser. A school that neglected these fundamentals in order to teach narrow techniques too early would produce workers unable to progress. This is why primary and secondary education in Cameroon, in both the English-speaking and the French-speaking subsystems, devote most of their time to languages, mathematics and the sciences.

Moreover, knowledge develops critical thinking and the ability to adapt. Trades change very quickly: digital technology has transformed banking, commerce and even agriculture, and some jobs that exist today will disappear tomorrow. A student who has only learnt a precise technique risks becoming obsolete, whereas one who has learnt to think, to analyse and to learn by himself can retrain throughout his life. In this sense, general culture is not a luxury but an investment in the future, and the "well-made head" praised by Montaigne is also the most adaptable worker.

Furthermore, school must transmit a common culture that builds the Nation. In a country of some two hundred and fifty ethnic groups and two official languages, school is one of the few places where young Cameroonians from all regions learn the same history, the same geography and the same civic values. Teaching bilingualism, national history and citizenship contributes directly to national integration. Law No. 98/004 of 14 April 1998 laying down guidelines for education in Cameroon thus assigns to education the intellectual, physical, civic and moral development of the child, which goes far beyond mere preparation for a job.

In short, by transmitting knowledge, school gives the individual solid foundations, a critical mind and a sense of belonging to the Nation. However, a school that ignored the world of work would produce frustrated graduates, which leads us to examine the need to prepare students for employment.

Nevertheless, in the face of graduate unemployment, school can no longer be indifferent to employment, and it must therefore reconcile the transmission of knowledge with professional preparation.

Firstly, there is a serious mismatch between training and employment in Cameroon. Universities produce many graduates in general fields such as law, economics or literature, while the economy lacks technicians in agriculture, building, maintenance, energy and digital services. As a result, many young people end up in the informal sector, often in jobs that have nothing to do with their studies. Aware of this problem, the authorities have long called for professionalisation: the Estates General of Education held in 1995 already recommended it, and the university reform of 1993 led to the creation of professional institutions such as the university institutes of technology.

Moreover, concrete measures can bring school closer to the world of work. Technical and vocational education, still too often regarded as a stream for weaker students, must be given greater value and better equipment. Internships, apprenticeships and partnerships with companies allow students to discover real working conditions, and the competency-based approach introduced in secondary school curricula aims precisely to link knowledge to real-life situations. In addition, teaching entrepreneurship can help young people create their own jobs rather than wait for employment in the public service.

Finally, the opposition between knowledge and employment is largely a false one. The best preparation for a job is a solid common core of knowledge, followed by progressive guidance towards vocational or academic streams according to each student's aptitudes. The 1998 law itself links the development of the child to his "harmonious integration into society", which includes economic life. In this balance, the teacher trained at the Higher Teacher Training College plays a decisive role: by linking each lesson to concrete applications, he shows students that knowledge is useful and that skills rest on knowledge.

In conclusion, the transmission of knowledge remains the primary mission of school, because it provides basic skills, develops critical thinking and builds national unity; however, in a context of graduate unemployment, school must also prepare students for employment through professionalisation, guidance and partnerships with the world of work. My answer is therefore that Cameroonian schools should not choose between the two, but should first transmit solid knowledge and then use it as the foundation of professional skills, training both the citizen and the worker. Yet can school alone solve the problem of youth unemployment if the economy itself does not create enough jobs?

sujet:
Practice paper – General culture

Can decentralisation strengthen national unity?

Discuss with particular reference to Cameroon.
corrige:
Since the constitutional reform of 18 January 1996, Cameroon has defined itself as a "decentralised unitary State". For a long time, this principle remained largely theoretical, but it gained new momentum after the Major National Dialogue of 2019, with the adoption of Law No. 2019/024 of 24 December 2019 bearing the General Code of Regional and Local Authorities and the election of the first regional councils in December 2020. Giving more powers and resources to councils and regions may, however, raise a fear: by strengthening territories, does the State not risk weakening the bonds that hold the Nation together? Can decentralisation, then, really strengthen national unity, or does it threaten it? We shall first examine the real risks that decentralisation poses to national unity; we shall then show that, provided certain conditions are met, it can become a powerful instrument of unity.

Decentralisation carries real risks for national unity, especially in a country as diverse as Cameroon.

Firstly, it may encourage identity withdrawal. When power is transferred to territories that often coincide with ethnic or linguistic areas, local political life may be dominated by the opposition between "natives" and "non-natives". The Constitution itself provides, in Article 57, that the regional council shall be chaired by an indigenous person of the region, a provision that some see as a recognition of local roots and others as a source of exclusion for citizens who have settled elsewhere. If local elected officials favour the "sons of the soil", decentralisation could divide citizens instead of uniting them.

Moreover, decentralisation may deepen inequalities between regions. Regions and councils do not have the same resources: those that host major economic activities, such as the Littoral region with the port of Douala, collect far more local revenue than rural councils in less developed areas. If competences are transferred without fair redistribution, the gap between rich and poor territories will widen, and the inhabitants of neglected regions may feel abandoned by the State. Such feelings of injustice are fertile ground for frustration and protest.

Furthermore, decentralisation may create conflicts of competence and weaken the authority of the State. Overlaps between councils, city councils, regions and the deconcentrated services of the State, represented by governors and senior divisional officers, can cause confusion and paralysis. More seriously, the crisis in the North-West and South-West regions since 2016 has shown that demands for autonomy can turn, in some groups, into calls for secession. A poorly controlled decentralisation could therefore be exploited by those who wish to break the unity of the country.

Thus, decentralisation is not without danger: it may encourage tribalism, widen regional inequalities and weaken State authority. Nevertheless, these risks depend largely on the way it is designed and implemented, which leads us to consider how it can, on the contrary, strengthen national unity.

However, when it is well designed and properly implemented, decentralisation is a tool of national unity, because unity is not uniformity.

Firstly, decentralisation brings decisions closer to citizens and thus strengthens their attachment to the State. Councils are better placed than distant central ministries to know local needs in terms of water supply, markets, primary schools, local roads or health centres. For instance, a council that builds a market shed or equips a primary school with benches responds more quickly to the needs of its inhabitants than a decision taken hundreds of kilometres away. When citizens see concrete results and take part in choosing their local representatives, they feel that the State listens to them. In this way, decentralisation reduces the frustration that feeds rejection of the State and turns citizens into actors of public life.

Moreover, decentralisation makes it possible to recognise diversity within unity. The 2019 Code granted a special status to the North-West and South-West regions, taking into account their Anglo-Saxon legal and educational heritage. Their regional assemblies include a House of Divisional Representatives and a House of Chiefs, and a Public Independent Conciliator is responsible for handling disputes between citizens and the administration. By acknowledging these specificities within the framework of a single State, the authorities send the message that one can be fully English-speaking, or attached to one's region, and fully Cameroonian at the same time.

Finally, the success of decentralisation depends on a number of conditions. Competences must be accompanied by a real transfer of resources, through the general decentralisation grant and the action of FEICOM, the fund that supports councils. Equalisation mechanisms must help the poorest regions to catch up. The supervisory control exercised by representatives of the State must ensure legality without stifling local initiative. Lastly, elected officials and local staff must be properly trained, which is the mission of institutions such as the Local Government Training Centre in Buea, and also a challenge for the future administrators trained at ENAM, who will have to support local authorities rather than replace them.

In conclusion, decentralisation does present risks for national unity, since it can encourage identity withdrawal, deepen inequalities between regions and create conflicts of competence. However, when it brings decisions closer to citizens, recognises the diversity of the country and is supported by adequate resources, fair equalisation and effective State control, it becomes a bond rather than a threat. My answer is therefore that decentralisation can strengthen national unity in Cameroon, on condition that it is conceived as a partnership between the State and the territories, and not as a competition between them. It remains to be seen whether young Cameroonians, who are often distant from local politics, will take ownership of this local democracy and make it the school of a stronger national citizenship.
